title: Tosafot
hookLine: Rashi's grandsons and their students add questions across the whole Talmud

lines: THE GRANDSONS ASK: DOES THIS FIT?
cards: A grandfather writes an explanation of the Talmud that his students learn from. His grandsons grow up with it. Then, with their own students, they do something bold.
They read his notes next to the Talmud, and next to other pages of the Talmud, and they start asking: does this really fit? What about the place where it says the opposite? Not to tear him down.
To finish the work. Their questions end up printed on the outer edge of the page, facing his.

teach.b: Tosafot. Additions. The comments printed on the outer margin of the Talmud page, written by a circle of scholars in France and Germany that began with Rashi's own family.
Among them was Rabbeinu Tam, one of Rashi's grandsons, whom you met in year three. First, how they work. Each comment opens like Rashi's, with a heading copied from the Gemara.
But where Rashi explains the line in front of you, Tosafot look across the whole Talmud.
This page says one thing, but another tractate seems to say the opposite. How can both stand? Then they work out an answer.

Second, they ask Rashi too. Back on the first page of Berakhot, Rashi said the evening Shema in synagogue, before dark, is a way to stand in prayer out of words of Torah, and the main duty is the bedtime Shema.
Tosafot push back. The bedtime Shema, they note, is said without the blessings that go with the Shema, and for a different purpose.
So they bring another explanation, in Rabbeinu Tam's name, that makes room for the early evening practice. A grandson answering his grandfather, on the very first page. Third, the spirit of it.
Respect, here, means taking someone seriously enough to question him. Tosafot never erase Rashi.
They sit opposite him on the page, and learners read both. Fourth, what that does to a learner. Rashi helps you understand the line.
Tosafot make you ask whether you understood it. The page needs both.

how: In a study hall, learners often read a passage of Gemara with Rashi first and then turn to Tosafot, whose questions across tractates are part of advanced Talmud study.

o: extra prayers added at the end of a service
questions and answers on the Talmud's outer margin
a list of corrections added to later printings

p: explains the line in front of you

s: Tosafot were written to replace Rashi
they sit opposite him on the page, and learners read both.
Tosafot question Rashi on the very first page of Berakhot
they push back on his reading of the evening Shema and bring an explanation in Rabbeinu Tam's name.
Tosafot only explain the page in front of them
they read each page against the rest of the Talmud and ask how both can stand.

games.q: you're one of Rashi's grandsons. you know his notes by heart, and you find a page elsewhere in the Talmud that seems to contradict his reading. what do you do?
o: write a question beside the text and work toward an answer.
rewrite his notes so the problem disappears.
games.why: that's Tosafot: questions written facing Rashi across the page, never erasing him. respect, here, means taking him seriously enough to ask.

practice: Bring to mind an explanation you received and never questioned, something a parent said about how the world works, and hold it with respect, the way the grandsons held Rashi.
Then ask one gentle Tosafot question: does this fit with everything else I know? You don't have to answer; you're adding, not erasing.

wordCard.voice: Tosafot. Additions: the questions and answers on the Talmud's outer margin, from Rashi's grandsons and their students, reading each page against the whole. Today's word.
